messages.subject: [statnet_help] question about importing vertex attributes
messages.body_plain:
Hank Green wrote:
> hi statnet guys...
>  
> hank here again, with another question that probably has a searingly 
> simple answer.
>  
> i have a set of vertex attributes saved as a tab delimited text file.
> i would like to assign the values in the text file to my 
> network vertices en mass.
>  
> i have read over the set.vertex.attributes help file, but am still not 
> sure exactly how to do this type of work from a file...
> (i assume i use the read.table function in some way, but i'm not 
> entirely sure)
>  
> thanks for the help, sorry i'm being dense...
>  

Here's one way to do it:

dat<-read.table("myfile",header=T)
for(i in 1:NROL(dat))
   mynet%v%names(dat)[i]<-dat[,i]

This assumes that you have a header row in "myfile" and that your 
network is called "mynet."  Other variants are possible.  (In fact, you 
can do this in one line, using an apply function....)

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] generating a predicted network
messages.body_plain:
Hi friends.
I'd like to generate a weighted graph where the edges
are the probabilities of a tie existing between vertices
based on the results of an ergm.

I know that the probabilities generated by an ergm are
for a given tie conditional on the rest of the network.
This being the case, simply using the parameter estimates
from the ergm to generate a predicted network doesn't seem
right.

To make things easier, my ergm is solely an analysis of
homophily, i.e., NetworkTie ~ edge + nodematch("race") + nodematch("sex") ...

Is there an established way to generate a predicted network?
Since I'm not doing any structural terms (e.g., triangle),
can I just use the ergm results?

Thank you very much.

Kind regards,
Brian

-- 
Brian Rubineau                             PhD Candidate, Organization Studies
brubineau@sloan.mit.edu                         MIT Sloan School of Management
tel: 617.253.6680                                   50 Memorial Drive, E52-511
fax: 810.963.2738                                         Cambridge, MA  02142

It looks like version 2.4.0 of R for the Mac has broken "statnet".
Updates to R often break packages, and it is advisable to reinstall packages after major updates to R.

In this case I have remade "statnet". If you try

"library(updatestatnet)"

from R it should update to version 1.0-10 (for the Mac) and resolve the difficulties.

Let me know how it goes.

Regards,

Mark

The "latentcov" term is what you want. For example,

samp.fit <- ergmm(samplike ~ latentcov(samegroup) + latent(k=2))

It is documented in "terms.ergmm" and there is an example in "ergmm".

Mark

messages.subject: [statnet_help] generating a predicted network
messages.body_plain:
Dear Brian,

Thanks for the question.

As your model is dyad independence you can obtain an expression analytically
using the coefficients in the same way as you do for logistic regression.
That is, in this case the conditional and unconditional probabilities are
the same.

It is easier to use the simulate command to generate, e.g., 1000 networks
from the fitted model and take the average sociomatrix from them. This is a
consistent estimate of the probabilities, and will work for an arbitrary
"ergm" model to boot.

I hope this helps.

Mark

Dear Statnet Help,

I've noticed that interpretation of statistical significance in ERGM
terms can be extremely different depending on whether you use the Wald
test (at least, that's what I think they are) P values reported in the
model summary or compare AICs of nested models; sometimes the addition
of an extra term contributes virtually nothing to improving the
likelihood, but the se of the term is very low. Has anyone done any
simulations for different kinds of dataset in order to come up with
guidelines?

Best
Simon

Hi Simon,

I have noticed similar effects like this at times, and have considered 
that I should at some point explore it more deeply.  Others on the statnet 
team can probably answer this more rigorously, but in my own casual use I 
tend to be more interested in the p-values than in the AIC or other model 
likelihood measures, since the former seem to be more stable across 
multiple repeated runs on the same data, for what seem like reasonable 
chain lengths.  We're looking at other measures of goodness of fit in 
terms of the degree to which models capture various network statistics 
that are not includedin the model.  However, I'm not aware of anyone 
delving very deeply into the question you asked specifically.  Perhaps you 
could take the first stab?

> increases, so taking action to reduce excess dependence (e.g., by using

connected clusters. I do have covariates that deal with some of the
clustering.

> took it out of the final version).  This is computationally expensive, 
> but avoids the assumption of an asymptotically log-quadratic likelihood 
> surface.

This would be pretty straightforward in my case. What about
nonparametric bootstrapping? What would the unit of sampling be?

> You can also employ approximate Bayesian inference, e.g., by 
> using posterior mode approximations as described in Gelman et al.

> a related family of models.

> test (at least, that's what I think they are) P values reported in the
> model summary or compare AICs of nested models; sometimes the addition
> of an extra term contributes virtually nothing to improving the
> likelihood, but the se of the term is very low. Has anyone done any
> simulations for different kinds of dataset in order to come up with
> guidelines?

FWIW, the method used to approximate the log-likelihood is (unless it 
has changed recently) generally less stable than the method used to 
obtain approximate standard errors.  Thus, the log-likelihood estimates 
can be pretty noisy in some cases.  On the other hand, the reported 
standard errors are based on the hessian of the (approximate) 
log-likelihood surface at the MLE, and may or may not represent true SEs 
for the parameters in question.  (Size asymptotics apply in the case of 
independent dyads, but otherwise there are no guarantees -- then again, 
asymptotics don't come with finite-sample guarantees anyway, so you may 
not be losing much.)

The pessimistic view is thus that you have a choice between a noisier 
estimate of a number which has a principled interpretation, or a cleaner 
estimate of a number which has an unprincipled interpretation.  The fact 
that the two choices can lead to different test results is not too 
surprising (although this is cold comfort from a practical standpoint). 
  There is reason to expect that both the noise and the quality of the 
asymptotic approximation will become worse as dyadic dependence 
increases, so taking action to reduce excess dependence (e.g., by using 
covariates where possible) may help.  You can also improve the quality 
of the log-likelihood estimate by increasing the number of simulation 
draws, as well as the number of refinement iterations which are 
performed (see the ergm help).

An alternative to both approaches is to employ a parametric bootstrap, 
as suggested in the recent Hunter and Handcock JCGS paper (unless they 
took it out of the final version).  This is computationally expensive, 
but avoids the assumption of an asymptotically log-quadratic likelihood 
surface.  You can also employ approximate Bayesian inference, e.g., by 
using posterior mode approximations as described in Gelman et al. 
(2004).  I've not done these with ERGMs yet, but have had good luck with 
a related family of models.

That doesn't exactly solve your problem (such is the nature of life at 
the bleeding edge), but perhaps it provides some useful background.  Now 
that we're finally getting a handle on how to parameterize and fit these 
models, I expect that more attention will be turned to problems such as 
these....

-Carter
